section.name: JSON Member Handling Examples
section.t: Some JSON parsers silently keep a single value for a repeated member name. Implementers can use a parser with duplicate-name detection or check decoded names as the parser emits them, before converting the object to a map. Checking the resulting map cannot detect duplicates that the parser already discarded. For the response, these envelope checks apply to the top-level JSON object. The claim_set string is validated separately under .
The following fragments illustrate member handling. Each fragment is added to an otherwise valid message unless indicated.

tr.td: Request with an unrecognized top-level member
Request with an unavailable attribute name
Process normally and omit the unavailable attribute.
Request with an unsupported query value
HTTP 200 response with an extra member
Ignore the extra member and apply all applicable response checks.
HTTP 200 response with a duplicate member
HTTP 200 response with an error member
Reject the response as a successful result, including as an empty result.

section.name: Claims Delivery
section.t: OpenID.Core governs claim destinations, omission rules, and the Aggregated Claims representation.

ol.li: The OP MUST apply the applicable request constraints to each response.
The OP MUST omit _claim_names entries for claims it cannot supply in an authorized, valid Claim Set.
The OP MUST limit each embedded JWT to claims the Subject authorizes for disclosure to that RP.
The OP MUST replace or omit any Claim Set with claims outside the RP's disclosure authorization.
The OP MUST preserve mappings for other claims it returns, including Distributed Claims.
The OP MUST preserve the sources that those mappings reference.
The OP MUST omit each _claim_sources entry that no remaining _claim_names entry references.
If _claim_names would be empty, the OP MUST omit both _claim_names and _claim_sources.
The OP MUST NOT forward CP error details to explain an omission.
The RP MUST enforce its application's required-claim policy before completing the requested operation.

section.t: The RP receives all claims in the embedded JWT, including claims without a mapping in _claim_names. specifies when the OP can use previously collected Claim Sets. The essential flag alone does not make an omission an authentication error under OpenID.Core.
For example, the RP requests birthdate and address in the ID Token:

The CP supplies only birthdate. The OP returns the following presentation. Only birthdate has a _claim_names mapping, and the response contains only the source referenced by that mapping. If the RP requires address for its operation, it does not complete that operation.

The decoded OP presentation below embeds the same CP-signed JWT received in claim_set in , without changing its compact JWS serialization. The inner JWS is abbreviated here. When the OP returns the Aggregated Claims in an ID Token, the normal ID Token requirements still apply.
The enclosing sub identifies the Subject at the OP. The CP's account_ref and acquisition nonce are not included in the embedded JWT or passed on as acquisition evidence to the RP.

ol.li: The OP SHOULD return Aggregated Claims in a Token Endpoint ID Token or a UserInfo response.

section.t: This limits the front-channel exposure described in .

ol.li: The OP MUST obtain Claim Sets from the CP's Claims Endpoint.
The OP MUST NOT substitute a Setup ID Token, a refreshed ID Token, or a UserInfo JWT.
The OP MUST validate each CP-signed Claim Set when collecting it.
The OP MUST validate each stored Claim Set before disclosing it.
The RP MUST validate each embedded CP-signed JWT before accepting any claim from it.

section.name: CP Metadata and Verification Keys
section.t: The following sources supply CP metadata and its verification keys.

ul.li: OpenID.Discovery supplies validated provider metadata and application keys via jwks_uri.
OpenID.Federation supplies application signing keys in resolved openid_provider metadata.
Trusted deployment configuration or a trust framework can provision metadata and keys for a CP issuer.

ol.li: The verifier MUST obtain the CP's metadata and verification keys from one of these sources.
The verifier MUST select a source according to its trust policy for the CP.
The verifier MUST NOT substitute Federation Entity Keys for the CP's application signing keys.
The verifier MUST match the JWT's iss exactly to the CP issuer in validated metadata or trusted configuration.
The verifier MAY use unverified iss for key resolution only as its issuer acceptance and network policies permit.
The verifier MUST associate the CP's metadata and keys with that issuer, including in caches.
The verifier MUST apply the applicable validity requirements to metadata and keys.
The verifier MUST apply the applicable trust reevaluation requirements to metadata and keys.
The verifier MUST NOT rely on key discovery or signature verification alone to trust a CP for claims.
The verifier MUST NOT rely on prior validation if the signing key becomes unavailable or untrusted.

li.t: In that case, the OP MUST obtain a replacement Claim Set from the CP or omit the affected set.
The CP MUST apply the key-to-algorithm binding rules in RFC8725 when signing Claim Sets.
The CP MUST publish each Claim Set signing key's algorithm in every advertised JWK's alg.
The CP SHOULD keep retired public keys available through its advertised key sources until their signed Claim Sets expire.
The CP SHOULD include its clock-skew allowance in that key retention period.
The CP MAY withdraw compromised keys earlier under its deployment's key revocation policy.

section.name: Signature Validation
section.t: RFC7515 governs signature verification.

ol.li: The verifier MUST require an asymmetrically signed JWS.
The verifier MUST determine its allowed algorithms before verifying the signature.
The verifier MUST require alg in both local policy and the CP's validated claims_signing_alg_values_supported.
At acquisition, the OP MUST match alg to the signing_alg bound to the collection operation.
The verifier MUST use a public key bound to the validated CP issuer for signature verification.
The verifier MUST honor key type, signing use, and algorithm restrictions when selecting a key.
The verifier MUST resolve any kid only within the CP's trusted key set.
The verifier MUST NOT trust a key source solely because the JWT header identifies it.
The verifier MUST bind each key to one algorithm using JWK alg or trusted issuer-specific configuration.
If the JWK includes alg, the verifier MUST match it to the JWT's alg.
The verifier MUST reject the Claim Set if it cannot establish the key's algorithm binding.

section.name: Claim Validation
section.t: The verifier checks claims after validating the signature. RFC7519 governs time claim types, expiration, and not-before processing.

ol.li: The verifier MUST require claims-aggregation+jwt in the protected header's typ.
The verifier MUST reject a Claim Set whose payload contains sub.
The verifier MUST require iss, aud, iat, and exp.
The verifier MUST require a non-empty string for iss.
The OP MUST validate the acquisition or stored binding under .
The verifier MUST require exactly one aud value as a string or single-element array.
The OP MUST match aud exactly to its client_id at the CP.
The RP MUST match aud exactly to the OP issuer it validated through OpenID Connect.
The verifier MUST compare issuer and audience identifiers without normalization.
The verifier MUST require exp to be later than iat.
The verifier MUST reject a JWT with an iat in the future.
The verifier MAY allow a small clock skew when comparing times to its clock.
The verifier MUST apply any clock-skew allowance consistently to iat, exp, and nbf.

section.t: The following requirements apply when the RP receives Aggregated Claims through UserInfo.

ol.li: The RP MUST use the validated OP issuer from the transaction that issued the access token.
The RP MUST NOT infer a new issuer from the CP JWT or an unsigned UserInfo response.
The RP MUST preserve the OP issuer's association with that access token.

section.t: The RP relies on the OP for Subject binding as described in . The RP follows the same clause when deciding whether to trust the CP.

ol.li: The RP MUST validate the Aggregated Claims structure according to OpenID.Core.
The RP MUST check that each mapped claim appears in its referenced JWT.
The RP MUST apply the validation rules for each claim it uses.
The OP MUST reject a Claim Set that fails any required check.
The OP MUST NOT store an invalid Claim Set.
The OP MUST NOT disclose an invalid Claim Set.
The RP MUST NOT use claims from an invalid Claim Set.
The RP MUST treat claims mapped to an invalid Claim Set as unavailable.
The RP MAY reject the entire enclosing response.
Profiles MAY require rejection of the entire enclosing response.

section.t: The verification rules in apply to every Claim Set the RP uses. specifies when the RP can complete the requested operation.

section.name: Local Freshness Policy and User-Directed Updates
section.t: The RP's acceptance checks include Claim Set validation and its freshness policy.

ol.li: The RP MUST apply its application's freshness requirements before using claims.
The RP MUST apply its acceptance checks to Claim Sets it uses after OP selection or a user-directed update.
The RP MAY enforce a maximum JWT age based on the CP-signed iat.
If a Claim Set is too old, the RP MUST treat its claims as unavailable for that use.
The RP SHOULD explain to the Subject when updated information is necessary.
The RP MAY direct the Subject to the OP's claim-management interface to request an update.

section.t: The Subject can retry the OpenID Connect interaction after an update. Retrying authentication alone does not require the OP to recollect claims.
IDA.Schema defines the verified_claims structure. Using it does not by itself implement the OpenID4IDA query protocol or external assertion format.
Implementations that support OpenID4IDA can use its existing request and validation mechanisms. For example, max_age constrains verification.time or another requested date or timestamp.

ol.li: The RP MUST evaluate assurance timestamps separately from the JWT's iat when it uses OpenID4IDA freshness constraints.
The OP MAY use supported constraints to select stored Claim Sets.

section.t: A new JWT does not show when the CP last verified the claims. Meeting a verification-age requirement can require renewed verification at the CP. Mapping constraints into a Claims Endpoint request requires a separate extension or profile. The base claims object accepts only null values. The OP can support OpenID4IDA without forwarding constraints or using them to select stored Claim Sets under this specification. OpenID4IDA still governs its implementers' query, filtering, and omission behavior.
The OpenID4IDA external assertion format uses typ=provided-claims+jwt and requires sub. That format prohibits aud and exp.

ol.li: The OP MUST NOT rewrite an existing signed assertion to convert it to this profile.

section.t: Interoperability with that external assertion format requires a separate profile.

section.name: General Security Considerations
section.t: The security considerations of OpenID.Core, OpenID.Federation, and RFC8725 apply.

Before verifying the signature, the verifier constrains algorithms and keys under and . This prevents a JWT header from selecting an unauthorized algorithm or causing use of a CP public key as a MAC secret.

ol.li: The CP SHOULD consider claim sensitivity, change rate, storage duration, and verification key retention when choosing Claim Set lifetimes.

section.t: Short lifetimes require more frequent collection, while long lifetimes extend the period during which previously issued attributes can be presented. Expiration limits the lifetime of the signed artifact. It does not guarantee that the underlying attributes remain current or that the CP's grant remains authorized. Key withdrawal can make a stored Claim Set unusable before its exp, as described in .

The type and claim rules in distinguish Claim Sets from ID Tokens and UserInfo JWTs. RFC8725 describes cross-JWT confusion. A separate URL or the presence or absence of nonce or auth_time does not by itself distinguish these JWTs.

section.name: Setup Transaction and Session Integrity
section.t: The issuer-based countermeasure in OAuth.Security.Update protects connections to multiple CPs. binds metadata to the selected issuer. checks that issuer before code exchange. That check also addresses the mix-up risk in RFC9700. preserves the selected client and any connection or tenant context.

PKCE binds the code to the OP's token request under . An attacker can still initiate Setup for the attacker's OP account and induce a victim to authorize access to the victim's CP account. PKCE alone does not detect this cross-user session fixation attack, described in Section 2.3 of OAuth.Security.Update, with countermeasures in Section 2.3.2. Before exchanging the code, the OP verifies the completion session's binding under . A valid state received through a URL is insufficient without this session validation. Comparing a previously stored CP subject identifier detects account changes. Checking for the same CP (iss, sub) on another OP account can also detect an attempted new binding when that CP identity is already known to the OP. Neither check establishes a relationship for a CP identity that has never been linked at the OP. The trust assumptions in continue to apply.

section.name: RP Request Integrity and Broker-Side Consent
section.t: The checks in apply to signed and unsigned requests.

The OP brokers requests between RPs and CPs using the broker-side consent approach in OAuth.Security.Update. The CP grant authorizes collection, and the Subject's authorization at the OP governs RP disclosure. covers both RP-triggered collection and reuse. The Subject can withdraw authorization under even if the CP grant remains valid. Pre-collection can keep the recipient RP and its activity timing from the CP.

An ID Token returned from the Authorization Endpoint can expose embedded CP-signed Claim Sets to browser scripts and front-channel response handling. Depending on the response mode and implementation, those artifacts can persist in URLs, including fragments, browser history, or application and diagnostic logs. Unlike an authorization code, the signed personal data can be copied and presented to other parties, subject to their acceptance checks. The back-channel delivery recommendation in reduces this exposure; it does not prevent an RP that receives a Claim Set from copying it. This is an additional reason to minimize front-channel exposure alongside the leakage risks discussed in Sections 4.2 and 4.3 of RFC9700.

section.name: Audience Binding
section.t: The Claim Set audience identifies the OP that obtained it. The RP checks that audience under and applies its CP trust policy.

ol.li: The CP MUST establish the client under before issuing a Claim Set.
The CP MUST NOT let another client use that client_id, including through a separate registration.

section.name: Cross-User Claim Substitution
section.t: A compromised or malicious OP can include a Claim Set for one Subject in a response for another Subject. The substituted Claim Set can have a valid CP signature and the expected OP audience. The RP's signature and audience checks therefore cannot detect this substitution. The trust model in relies on the OP to preserve the account binding through collection, storage, and disclosure. A Federation Trust Mark can attest to an OP's compliance with operational requirements. It does not prove the account binding for a particular response.

section.name: Operation and Response Binding
section.t: The collection nonce correlates an authenticated CP response with a pending OP operation; it is not an access credential or an issuance-idempotency key. The CP may process a retried request more than once, but the OP accepts at most one response for its pending operation. A holder of a stolen bearer token can request additional Claim Sets with new nonces, so a CP nonce database would not prevent that use. TLS server authentication and the token protections in address that threat.

ol.li: The OP MUST validate the CP endpoint's TLS server identity.

section.t: Deployments can impose issuance rate limits without making every CP maintain a shared nonce-replay database.

The OP binds the selected signing algorithm to the operation before sending the request and checks the returned JWT against it. A request or response that traverses an untrusted internal processing boundary needs integrity protection across that boundary as described in ; token sender-constraining alone does not authenticate arbitrary JSON request or response bodies across such a boundary.

section.name: Trusted Collection and Protected Handoffs
section.t: The trusted collection boundary includes the components the deployment relies on to preserve two inputs:

ul.li: The authenticated CP response.
The operation context that the OP selected independently.

section.t: Those components preserve both inputs until a trusted component validates the response and protects the resulting binding record. The deployment identifies which components it trusts and which compromises it aims to withstand. Common ownership, an OP-managed label, and the number of TLS connections are insufficient on their own. Access controls, account and tenant separation, and authenticated handoffs help enforce the boundary.

The base protections suffice when a trusted OP collector receives the response over authenticated TLS, checks it under , and protects the complete association between the account and the JWT. The account check compares account_ref with the CP's sub from the validated Setup ID Token. The CP-signed JWT contains no CP Subject Identifier that could independently confirm the association.

A TLS-terminating gateway can be part of the trusted collector if the deployment trusts it to preserve the response and operation context. A deployment that aims to withstand compromise of that gateway places it outside the trusted collection boundary.

A trusted collector can validate the response and protect the complete binding record before handing it to a queue, cache, or object store outside the boundary. The trusted consumer then verifies that record. An extra CP signature is unnecessary for that handoff alone.

An OP MAC, signature, or suitably bound authenticated encryption can protect the exact JWT together with its OP account, CP identifiers, and acquisition context. requires protection of the association as well as the JWT. On backup restoration, the OP applies the current deletion and withdrawal decisions under . An authentic older record can predate those decisions.

section.name: Additional CP-Origin Evidence
section.t: An additional CP signature can help when a TLS terminator outside the trusted collection boundary can alter the response before an honest OP component validates it.

For example, a gateway could pair a valid Claim Set for CP account B with an acquisition envelope for account A. B's JWT can have the expected OP audience, requested attributes, and selected signing algorithm. The envelope can carry A's account_ref and pending operation nonce. The checks of the account reference and the JWT's issuer, audience, signature, and lifetime can all pass because the JWT has no CP Subject Identifier. If the gateway kept B's account_ref, the account comparison would fail. A MAC that the OP adds after substitution protects the pairing it received. It cannot establish that the CP supplied that pairing.

The trusted validator needs to verify that the CP supplied the association between the account and the exact Claim Set. A CP-signed envelope or receipt can provide that evidence. An authenticated connection from the CP to the trusted validator can also protect it if the connection keeps the plaintext from the intermediary. The need for extra evidence depends on which components the deployment trusts.
An independently authorized auditor can also need evidence that the CP associated an account with a particular JWT. The relevant evidence depends on the audit question and policy:

ul.li: An OP signature can provide the evidence if the audit policy accepts records that the OP creates.
The existing Claim Set signature shows which attributes the CP signed.
A CP-signed receipt can show which account the CP associated with the Claim Set. This is useful when the auditor needs evidence from the CP.

section.t: This audit use requires a separately authorized purpose for access to stable CP account references and acquisition records. That access also requires minimization and retention controls. Normal RP disclosure follows .

section.name: Receipt Scope and Reuse Limits
section.t: A separate receipt profile would need to bind the following values to the exact signed Claim Set or to a collision-resistant commitment to it:

ul.li: A distinct receipt purpose.
The CP issuer.
The recipient OP.
The CP-derived account reference.
The acquisition operation nonce.

section.t: The OP uses one identifier here. Its Entity Identifier, Issuer Identifier, and CP-facing client_id are equal. A commitment would specify its algorithm and byte representation. Using the exact compact JWS avoids reserializing decoded claims. The proof protects the pairing only if it covers both the account reference and the JWT or its commitment.

A receipt profile would also need to specify trusted key and algorithm selection, pending-operation checks, and what to do if a required proof is missing or stripped. It would define how to handle empty results. This specification defines no receipt format, parameter, or mandatory additional CP signature.

A verified receipt authenticates a CP statement under the accepted signing key and policy. It cannot prove that the CP sent an HTTP response or that the OP received or validated it. It cannot establish the truth of the CP's account association or the Subject's consent to later RP disclosure. An issuance timestamp does not prove delivery or a new identity check.

The OP still needs its protected account binding. A receipt cannot restore a lost association with an authenticated OP account. A malicious OP can still violate . A receipt also cannot prevent misuse of stolen tokens, suppression of responses, or rollback of authorization state.

A signature provides integrity and evidence of origin. Anyone with the OP's public key can encrypt to it, so encryption to the OP alone cannot establish CP origin. A deployment that needs both confidentiality and CP-origin integrity across a boundary needs a design that protects the contents and authenticates the CP.

The Subject's authorization governs disclosure, including when the OP stores encrypted data or holds a receipt. The Aggregated Claims response excludes acquisition receipts. Storage, audit access, and backup handling of receipts remain sensitive-data processing.

If a receipt profile sets an initial acceptance deadline, a late receipt cannot establish a new acquisition binding. When the OP validates acquisition in time and preserves the binding in a protected record, expiry of that deadline alone does not require CP contact or suspension of an otherwise acceptable stored Claim Set.

A receipt within its acceptance window does not extend the inner JWT's exp. Current key, signature, audience, trust, freshness, and Subject authorization checks still apply. These rules concern acquisition and storage. They add no presentation-time CP status check and leave the grant-revocation rules in in effect.

section.name: CP Credential Exposure and Claim Set Replay
section.t: Pre-collection permits an OP to hold a grant that covers future Subject-authorized uses beyond a single RP request. The least-privilege requirements in and limit requested access. Downscoping an access token does not by itself reduce the authority of the original refresh token. The protections in and address the resulting concentration of credentials and personal data at the OP.

The assertion audience restriction in implements the preferred audience-injection countermeasure in Section 2.1.2.1 of OAuth.Security.Update. The OP's Entity Identifier is its client_id at every CP, so uniqueness of client identifiers across CPs is not an available countermeasure. Using different authentication keys for different CPs can provide additional isolation only when each CP's accepted key set is also restricted accordingly. Publishing several keys in a common RP key set does not by itself establish that isolation.

The OP Entity manages the client authentication keys in this profile. An app on a device acts as the Entity's user interface or agent. The CP resolves one client identity and one RP metadata object for the OP's Entity Identifier. This profile does not define separate enrollment or authentication bindings for each device instance.

Sharing one authentication private key across devices increases the risk of key extraction. Listing all device keys in the common RP JWK Set can make that set grow without bound. It can reveal how many devices the OP uses and how often devices are added or removed. The CP still resolves the same client identity for those keys.

A confidential client can run on a device. Device-generated keys and registration for each instance can support secure client authentication. Combining these with the common Entity Identifier, OP issuer, and RP metadata requires a separate profile.

Such a profile could use Explicit Registration or Dynamic Client Registration for each instance. It could also let the OP Entity attest to each instance's key while it keeps the Entity Identifier as client_id. The profile would need to define the binding between each instance, its credentials, client_id, and the OP issuer. It would also need rules for selecting the authentication method. Giving an instance a different client_id while keeping a common OP issuer would change the identity relationship in this base profile. These instance profiles are outside the scope of this specification.

Client authentication and sender-constrained CP access tokens protect collection, not the subsequent presentation of a signed Claim Set. A Claim Set's audience identifies the OP, not an individual RP or presentation. An RP or another holder can copy that JWT and send it elsewhere. To accept the Claim Set, the recipient validates the enclosing response and the Claim Set under . The recipient also relies on the account binding described in . Possession of the embedded JWT alone does not authenticate the Subject. A short Claim Set lifetime limits the exposure period. A holder can still copy or reuse the Claim Set before expiration.

Under the trust model in , the RP relies on the OP's account binding and disclosure controls. These protections neither require per-presentation CP contact nor cause CP grant revocation to invalidate stored Claim Sets. Storage remains under the Subject's control within the limits described in .

section.name: Freshness and Revocation Limits
section.t: The CP's signed iat establishes the JWT's age for freshness checks.

ol.li: The verifier MUST NOT substitute an OP collection timestamp or enclosing ID Token iat for the CP-signed iat.

section.t: A CP can issue a new JWT containing attributes verified earlier. Applications needing freshness of identity verification or evidence can use the corresponding signed data and validation rules in OpenID4IDA, as described in .

The Subject controls a signed Claim Set held by the OP. CP grant or token revocation, including unilateral revocation, affects future collection. The Subject can continue to present previously issued Claim Sets until expiration, subject to this profile's validation and acceptance rules. describes the Subject's control over further disclosure at the OP.

A CP can choose a short lifetime when the underlying attributes can change quickly. An application that needs prompt status updates, such as for a revoked driver's license, can use a separate authenticated status mechanism and an acceptance policy for the issued Claim Set. Offline verification checks the signed Claim Set. It cannot establish that the attributes still reflect the current state. A current status check supplements that verification and concerns the issued Claim Set rather than the collection grant.

section.name: OP Visibility and Reliance on Subject Instructions
section.t: The OP processes the contents of Claim Sets from CPs and knows which RPs receive them. This combination can reveal attributes and relationships across services. In a deployment where a third party operates the OP and can access that processing or its records, the Subject places substantial trust in that operator. Encryption at rest protects stored data against some compromises; it does not by itself hide data from the OP while processing it. A distributed-claims deployment does not necessarily hide information from the OP either; visibility depends on which components actually obtain and process the data.

At Setup, the Subject authorizes the CP to release claims to the OP for future use under the Subject's direction. The CP relies on the OP to enforce the later RP-specific authorization in . A CP signature authenticates the issued data; it does not prove that the OP obtained authorization for a particular disclosure. Federation trust and policy information can inform a trust decision, but do not by themselves prove that the OP honored the Subject's instructions in an individual transaction.

The least-privilege and disclosure requirements in , , and limit what the OP obtains and discloses. In particular, the RP receives all claims in an embedded signed JWT, including claims not listed in _claim_names. The OP cannot remove individual claims from that JWT while preserving the CP's signature. A deployment seeking stronger limits on OP visibility or finer-grained disclosure needs an appropriate architecture or extension, rather than relying on storage encryption alone.

section.name: Correlation and Transferable Signed Data
section.t: The OP uses the CP's stable Subject Identifier for account binding. The RP-facing Claim Set omits that identifier. Pairwise identifiers at the CP would otherwise be scoped to the OP's Sector Identifier rather than to each downstream RP, as specified in Section 8.1 of OpenID.Core. Omitting the CP sub removes that direct downstream identifier; it does not guarantee unlinkability. Authorized identifying attributes can still correlate Subjects, and a CP can recognize information it issued when an RP shares it. The OP's pairwise identifiers in enclosing responses do not hide the inner JWT's contents.

When the OP reuses a Claim Set, it sends the same CP-signed JWT. An RP can compare the JWTs it receives in different presentations. RPs that share the JWTs they receive can also compare them across services. A matching JWT, including its signature, lets these recipients correlate the presentations. Different enclosing OP responses leave a reused inner JWT intact. Correlation by JWT comparison can therefore occur even when other identifiers are ephemeral or pairwise.
Recipients can also correlate newly issued JWTs through stable identifiers, identifying combinations of claims, or distinctive timestamps.

An RP can also pass a CP-signed JWT to a third party that can independently verify the CP's signature and the signed contents. This makes disclosure of signed personal data more consequential than disclosure of an unauthenticated assertion. The signature is evidence of what the CP issued, not proof that the Subject presented it to a particular RP or that the attributes remain current. The base format does not cryptographically prevent onward transfer. The Subject's controls at the OP cannot recover copies already held by RPs.

Selective disclosure can reduce the attributes revealed to a recipient, but does not by itself ensure unlinkability. For example, Section 10.1 of SD-JWT explains that recipients can correlate reuse of an issuer-signed credential and that colluding issuers and verifiers can recognize the same credential. SD-JWT is an example for future profiles, not a format introduced by this specification. Such profiles would need compatible subject-binding, audience, consent, and verification rules.

section.name: Pre-Collection, Batch Issuance, and On-Demand Issuance
section.t: Pre-collection and reuse of stored Claim Sets can reduce the CP's visibility into when the Subject uses an RP. If an RP asks the Subject for fresher claims, the Subject can request an update. The OP can then request a new Claim Set from the CP.
The CP can observe when Claims Endpoint requests arrive and how often they arrive. If those requests follow RP activity, the CP can use that pattern to infer when the Subject uses an RP.
The following recommendations apply when the OP seeks the Subject's collection or disclosure authorization.

ol.li: The OP SHOULD explain that reusing a signed JWT can link presentations.
The OP SHOULD explain that updates can reveal RP activity timing to the CP.

section.t: The Subject can then choose whether to authorize reuse or request an update, subject to the RP's acceptance policy. describes privacy policies and rate limits for user-directed updates.

Reuse avoids a Claims Endpoint call for each presentation. The CP can still observe activity through information shared by RPs or retrieval of metadata, verification keys, or status. Valid metadata and key caches tied to the issuer can reduce some such contact, subject to the requirements in .

An alternative design can pre-issue a batch of distinct credentials for one-time use, combining advance collection with avoidance of a common reused artifact. This introduces inventory and replenishment requirements. Section 10.1 of SD-JWT describes batch issuance for presentation and verifier-verifier unlinkability, including the need to avoid other common identifiers and timing values. It does not solve issuer-verifier collusion.

With this profile, the Subject can instead request a newly issued Claim Set for a use, without a CP sub in the presented JWT. This avoids maintaining a stock of unused credentials, but requires CP availability and continued willingness to issue, and exposes issuance timing to the CP. It does not require revealing the RP's identity to the CP. The correlation risks for newly issued Claim Sets are described in .

The stable account-binding identifier remains in the OP-facing acquisition envelope. The OP validates it against the Setup ID Token, then discloses only the inner JWT. The new endpoint avoids changing UserInfo's requirement that its sub match the ID Token sub. Using a refreshed ID Token itself would not provide that separation: Section 12.2 of OpenID.Core requires its issuer, subject, and audience to remain those of the original ID Token.

This specification introduces no batch issuance protocol and does not require a newly issued JWT per presentation. Reuse of stored Claim Sets and user-directed updates remain Subject choices, subject to RP acceptance policy. These issuance and reuse tradeoffs are not unique to either an OP-mediated or issuer-holder-verifier architecture.

section.name: Subject Control of Retention and Disclosure
section.t: The controls in let the Subject distinguish stored data from collection and disclosure permissions. They complement the CP's grant-management interface: revoking a CP grant does not retract issued Claim Sets, while withdrawal at the OP controls further OP disclosure. Neither operation retracts data already received by an RP. A Subject may retain a Claim Set as a personal record even after it expires; expiration restricts valid use rather than imposing deletion. The safeguards in address the resulting storage risks without imposing a protocol retention deadline or a particular archival encryption design.

Disclosure history can help the Subject identify RPs that already received their data, including when seeking deletion from those RPs. That history is itself sensitive personal data and remains subject to protection, minimization, and Subject deletion controls in . Export can give the Subject an independent copy of an issued artifact, but does not remove the transferability or correlation risks described in .

section.name: Other Protocol Elements
section.t: The account_ref, nonce, claims, signing_alg, and claim_set members are defined within this API's JSON request and response objects. They are not new top-level JWT claims or new Authorization or Token Endpoint parameters, and this specification requests no registrations for them in those registries. Existing names in other registries do not supply their API semantics. No new JOSE header parameter, signing algorithm, or structured syntax suffix is defined. The existing typ header, RS256 algorithm, +jwt suffix, JWT claims, and OAuth token/error mechanisms are reused. No new client capability metadata or OAuth error value is registered by this specification.
